comparison.note: Both mean extremely impressive and often work in the same sentence: “The view was magnificent/spectacular.” Learn common combinations rather than forcing a strict distinction. Spectacular also describes dramatic results, including a spectacular failure; magnificent normally expresses praise.

senses.definition: Extremely impressive or striking, especially to look at; also remarkable in scale or result.

term: incentive / motive / motivation / drive / cue / trigger / stimulus / impulse / encouragement
tts_text: incentive. motive. motivation. drive. cue. trigger. stimulus. impulse. encouragement

senses.definition: Something that encourages an action, often a reward or benefit.
senses.example: The bonus gives employees an incentive to improve performance.

senses.common_patterns: an incentive to + verb; offer/provide an incentive; tax incentives

situations.situation: You explain what makes work worthwhile.
situations.examples: “The bonus is an incentive to work harder.” / “The bonus gives me motivation to work harder.”
situations.guidance: Incentive names the encouraging benefit; motivation can describe the desire or reason it creates.

situations.situation: You describe a reason or determination.
situations.examples: “What was his motive for hiding it?” / “She has the drive to finish it.”
situations.guidance: Motive fits a reason behind an action; drive fits determination. Motivation can also refer to either reasons or willingness.

situations.situation: Something signals or sets off an action.
situations.examples: “That was my cue to leave.” / “Stress is a trigger for my headaches.” / “The policy provides a stimulus to investment.”
situations.guidance: Cue fits a signal; trigger fits a reaction starting; stimulus is broader and often scientific or economic.

situations.situation: You describe an urge or support.
situations.examples: “I resisted the impulse to buy it.” / “Her encouragement helped me keep going.”
situations.guidance: Impulse is a sudden urge; encouragement is supportive input.

comparison.note: These belong to related contexts, but are not nine interchangeable words for motivation. Incentive is something that makes acting worthwhile; motive is a reason behind an action. Motivation and drive overlap for willingness or determination. A cue is a signal; a trigger sets off a reaction; stimulus is broader and common in scientific/economic discussion. An impulse is a sudden urge; encouragement is supportive input. Start with familiar combinations: incentive to work, motive for lying, motivation to study, drive to succeed, cue to leave, trigger for headaches, stimulus to investment, impulse to buy, words of encouragement.

senses.common_patterns: motivation to + verb; motivation for + action; lack/lose motivation

senses.definition: Strong motivation or determination to achieve something.

senses.definition: A journey in a car or another road vehicle.

senses.definition: Operate a car or another motor vehicle.

senses.definition: Cause or strongly motivate an action, change, or result.

senses.definition: A signal that tells someone to act or helps them interpret a situation.

senses.common_patterns: a stimulus to + activity; respond to a stimulus; plural stimuli

senses.definition: A sudden urge to act, often without planning.

senses.common_patterns: an impulse to + verb; on impulse; resist an impulse

senses.definition: Support that gives someone confidence or makes them more willing to act.

senses.definition: Tell someone confidently that something is true or will happen.
senses.example: I assured her that we could meet the deadline.

senses.common_patterns: assure someone that + clause; assure someone of + noun

situations.examples: “I assured her that everything was fine.” / “I reassured her that everything was fine.”
situations.guidance: Both work; reassure explicitly addresses worry or doubt.

situations.situation: You distinguish comfort from a promise.
situations.examples: “I can reassure you that we’re doing our best, but I can’t guarantee success.”
situations.guidance: Guarantee commits to an outcome or certainty; reassurance need not do that.

comparison.note: Assure and reassure overlap when a confident statement reduces worry: “I assured/reassured her that everything was fine.” Reassure explicitly addresses worry or doubt. Guarantee is a stronger commitment to an outcome or certainty: “I can reassure you that we’re doing our best, but I can’t guarantee success.” Use assure/reassure + PERSON + that-clause; guarantee can take a that-clause directly.

senses.definition: a promise that something will happen or meet a standard.

situations.situation: An old API is no longer recommended.

situations.guidance: Discouraged use; not necessarily removed.

situations.examples: “Cars depreciate as they get older.”
situations.guidance: Depreciate describes value or accounting.

comparison.note: These three verbs are not synonyms. Deprive means deny something needed or valued; deprecate means discourage software use or formally disapprove; depreciate concerns monetary value or accounting. “The noise deprived me of sleep.” “We deprecated the old API.” “Cars depreciate.” A deprecated feature can still work; the status does not itself mean removal.

senses.common_patterns: deprecate an API/feature; a deprecated method

senses.definition: Reduce an asset’s recorded value over time in accounting.
senses.example: The company depreciates its equipment over five years.

senses.common_patterns: depreciate in value; depreciate equipment over five years

term: compromise / meet halfway / concede / give in / back down
pronunciation:
compromise: /ˈkɑmprəmaɪz/
meet halfway: /mit ˌhæfˈweɪ/
concede: /kənˈsid/
give in: /ɡɪv ˈɪn/
back down: /bæk ˈdaʊn/
tts_text: compromise. meet halfway. concede. give in. back down

senses.definition: an agreement reached by accepting less than originally wanted.
senses.example: We reached a compromise on the deadline.

senses.common_patterns: reach a compromise; compromise with someone on something; compromise security

situations.examples: “We compromised on the deadline.” / “We met each other halfway on the deadline.”
situations.guidance: Both work for mutual adjustment.

situations.examples: “They conceded on the deadline.”
situations.guidance: Concede can mean yield something after resisting.

situations.examples: “I concede that your approach is simpler.”
situations.guidance: Concede that + clause means admit a point; it need not mean accept a demand.

situations.examples: “She finally gave in.” / “She finally backed down.”
situations.guidance: Often overlapping; neither requires a mutual compromise.

situations.situation: An action puts something at risk.
situations.examples: “Sharing passwords compromises security.”
situations.guidance: Compromise also means weaken or endanger.

comparison.note: Compromise and meet someone halfway often describe the same mutual adjustment. Concede can mean admit a point or yield something. Give in and back down often overlap for stopping resistance; neither requires both sides to adjust. Compromise security means put security at risk, not negotiate.

senses.definition: accept less than originally wanted to reach agreement.
senses.example: We compromised on the deadline.

senses.definition: weaken or put something at risk.
senses.example: Sharing passwords can compromise security.

senses.definition: Accept part of another person's wishes so both sides can agree.
senses.example: If you can extend the deadline, I'll meet you halfway on the scope.

senses.common_patterns: meet someone halfway; meet each other halfway

senses.definition: Admit that something is true, or yield something after resisting.
senses.example: I concede that your approach is simpler.

senses.common_patterns: concede that + clause; concede a point; concede defeat

senses.definition: Stop resisting and agree to a demand or temptation.
senses.example: I finally gave in and agreed to help.

senses.common_patterns: give in to + pressure/demand/temptation

senses.definition: Withdraw a position or demand after opposition.
senses.example: She refused to back down on the deadline.

senses.common_patterns: back down on/from + position/demand; refuse to back down

term: responsible for / accountable for / answerable to / in charge of
pronunciation:
responsible for: /rɪˈspɑnsəbəl fɔr/
accountable for: /əˈkaʊntəbəl fɔr/
answerable to: /ˈænsərəbəl tu/
in charge of: /ɪn ˈtʃɑrdʒ əv/
tts_text: responsible for. accountable for. answerable to. in charge of

senses.definition: Having a duty, causing something, or bearing responsibility for a result.
senses.example: I'm responsible for reviewing pull requests.

synonyms.note: for answerability, not all duty/cause uses

senses.definition: Be the cause of something.
senses.example: A faulty sensor was responsible for the shutdown.

senses.definition: Bear responsibility or blame for a result.
senses.example: You’ll be held responsible for any mistakes.

senses.common_patterns: be responsible for + noun/V-ing; hold someone responsible for + result

situations.examples: “You’ll be held responsible for mistakes.” / “You’ll be held accountable for mistakes.”
situations.guidance: Both work; no strict distinction needed.

situations.examples: “I’m responsible for reviewing code.”
situations.guidance: Responsible for + noun/V-ing.

situations.situation: You name who you answer to.
situations.examples: “I’m accountable to my manager for the release.” / “I’m answerable to my manager for the release.”
situations.guidance: To introduces the person; for introduces the result or action.

situations.examples: “Maya is in charge of the project.”
situations.guidance: Management; she may also be responsible and accountable.

situations.examples: “A sensor was responsible for the failure.”
situations.guidance: Responsible also describes causes; a sensor cannot justify its actions.

comparison.note: Responsible for and accountable for often mean essentially the same thing for actions or results. “You’ll be held responsible/accountable for mistakes” is natural either way. Accountable makes explaining or justifying actions more explicit. Answerable to and accountable to name who you answer to; answerable for and accountable for name what you answer for. In charge of describes management and can overlap with both responsibility and accountability. Responsible also describes causes: “A faulty sensor was responsible for the failure”; accountable would be unusual for a sensor.

senses.definition: Responsible for actions or results and expected to explain or justify them.
senses.example: I'm accountable for the release outcome.

senses.common_patterns: be accountable for + noun/V-ing; be accountable to + person/body; hold someone accountable

senses.definition: Required to explain or justify your actions to a person or organization.
senses.example: The director is answerable to the board.

senses.common_patterns: be answerable to + person/body; be answerable for + action/result

senses.definition: Managing, directing, or having control over something.
senses.example: Maya is in charge of the project.

senses.common_patterns: be in charge of + noun/V-ing; put someone in charge of something

observed_forms: responsible for / accountable for / answerable to / in charge of

senses.definition: Acknowledge an earlier point and introduce a limitation or contrasting consideration.
senses.example: The tool is useful. That said, we still need to review its output.

synonyms.note: marks contrast without necessarily acknowledging the prior point

senses.common_patterns: statement. That said, + contrasting clause.

situations.situation: You add a limitation to an earlier claim.
situations.examples: “The tool is useful. That said, we still need to review its output.”
situations.guidance: That said qualifies the earlier point.

situations.examples: “Let’s say the server receives a thousand requests per second. How would we scale it?”
situations.guidance: Let’s say introduces an assumption; it does not itself mark contrast.

comparison.note: That said qualifies an earlier claim; let’s say introduces an example or assumption. “Remote work saves time. That said, it can feel isolating.” versus “Remote work saves time. Let’s say you save an hour a day—that adds up.” A reservation here means a concern or qualification, not a booking.

senses.definition: Introduce an assumed situation or illustrative example.
senses.example: Let’s say the server receives a thousand requests per second. How would we scale it?

synonyms.note: introduces examples without necessarily making an assumption

senses.common_patterns: let’s say + clause; let’s say + hypothetical amount. “Let’s say $500.”

tts_text: sentence. condemn. a convict. to convict. charge

senses.definition: officially impose a punishment in court.
senses.example: The judge sentenced him to three years in prison for fraud.

senses.common_patterns: sentence someone to + punishment; for + offense; receive/serve a prison sentence; write a sentence.

situations.examples: “Prosecutors charged him with fraud.”
situations.guidance: Charge someone with a crime; this does not establish guilt.

situations.situation: You report a finding of guilt.
situations.examples: “He was convicted of fraud.”
situations.guidance: Convict someone of a crime.

situations.examples: “The judge sentenced him to three years in prison.”
situations.guidance: Sentence someone to a punishment.

situations.examples: “The judge condemned his behavior.”
situations.guidance: Condemn normally expresses disapproval; the formal legal use also permits condemned to death.

comparison.note: Charge is an accusation; convict is a finding of guilt; sentence imposes punishment. A person can be charged without later being convicted. Condemn usually expresses strong disapproval; its formal legal sense also permits “condemned to death.” Sentence is the usual neutral verb for reporting a prison term. This comparison focuses on the legal sense of charge; its other everyday senses are outside this proposal.

senses.definition: a punishment imposed by a court.
senses.example: He received a three-year prison sentence.

senses.definition: a grammatical unit expressing a statement, question, or other complete construction.
senses.example: Write one sentence using the new word.

senses.definition: To express strong disapproval of someone or something, usually for moral reasons.
senses.example: The board condemned the use of customer data without consent.

senses.definition: To sentence someone to a punishment or force someone into an unpleasant condition.
senses.example: The ruling condemned thousands of families to years of uncertainty.

synonyms.note: used specifically for a legal punishment

senses.definition: To officially declare a building unsafe or unfit for use.
senses.example: Inspectors condemned the apartment building after the fire.

senses.common_patterns: condemn + person/thing; condemn someone for + wrongdoing; condemn something as + description; condemn someone to + punishment/condition.

senses.definition: officially find someone guilty of a crime.
senses.example: He was convicted of fraud.

synonyms.note: to the noun, not every prisoner has been convicted

antonyms.note: of the verb: acquit someone of a charge

senses.common_patterns: convict someone of + crime; be convicted of + crime; an escaped convict.

senses.definition: a person found guilty of a crime, especially one serving a prison sentence.
senses.example: The novel follows an escaped convict.

senses.definition: formally accuse someone of a crime.
senses.example: Prosecutors charged him with fraud.

synonyms.note: broader and uses accuse someone of something

senses.common_patterns: charge someone with + crime/V-ing; be charged with + crime; face a charge; charges against someone.

senses.definition: a formal accusation of a crime.
senses.example: He faces a fraud charge.
